prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at the magic wavelength brought atomic frequency standards to the 10^-18 regime

statement.case_for: I keep B022 as my single preferred part after the full first-round exchange. The case is a datable invention with a precise conceptual step (trapping many neutral atoms at the magic wavelength so that the lattice light shift cancels) and a decisive realisation (strontium lattice clocks at fractional uncertainties near 10^-18, with the many-body regime in Ye's dense-lattice work). It has been reproduced with Sr, Yb and Hg in many laboratories and compared over fibre links, and the uses are already delivered: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on drifting constants, dark-matter searches, and the groundwork for a redefinition of the second. That matches the criterion I described in Tokyo, a discovery or invention with the topic and the people responsible for the original work identifiable. The chair asks whether the citation can be worded so it does not cover optical clocks in general. I think it can and must: it names the lattice, the magic wavelength and the 10^-18 regime, so it leaves single-ion clocks (2012) and the comb (2005) where they are. On the Katori and Ye split, Katori is the concept and the first strontium lattice clock, Ye is the record accuracy and the many-body and comparison work; the citation says 'invention and realisation' so both halves are credited and neither is made to carry the other. Nothing in round 1 has moved me to a different configuration, but it has sharpened what I am prepared to rest on.
statement.case_against: My reservations are unchanged, and I now think two of them are real rather than rhetorical. First, the category question: a record in accuracy is an instrument-level result, and the committee should be honest that the new knowledge about nature comes through its uses, not through the clock itself. Second, the credit tail. Lemonde, Takamoto, the Yb and Hg groups and Ye's JILA collaborators are outside a two-name prize, and the Katori and Ye contest over who first reached 10^-18 is real. A citation worded around invention and realisation answers part of this but not all of it. Third, the B045 supporters are right that topological band theory reorganised a whole field, and breadth of influence is a legitimate criterion that I am setting against attribution clarity, not dismissing. The SI second has not been redefined, and while I do not treat that as a precondition, a committee that wanted extra assurance of culmination could reasonably wait a year or two.

responses.point: Argues that clean attribution does not make a stronger case, and that topological band theory introduced a classification principle that spread across materials, photonics and devices, whereas a clock is a gain in precision inside a field prized in 2005 and 2012.
responses.response: This is the strongest argument against my position and I have tried to weigh it on its terms. I agree that breadth of conceptual influence is a legitimate criterion and that tidy credit should not decide first place alone. Where I differ is that the question for me is what is being rewarded and who did it, and for the quantum spin Hall effect that is exactly where the case is least settled: the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal directed Molenkamp's experiment, Zhang has died, and the 3D and QAH strands are left out. You propose to state this openly in the citation. I respect that, but a citation limited to the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 classification will be read as the headline of topological insulators, and the omission will still be the first thing said about it. I also do not accept that the clock is only a precision gain: the magic-wavelength lattice opened a measurement regime in which relativistic effects appear across a millimetre, and I count that as new access to nature. I move no further than ranking B045 as my first alternative, ahead of B030.

responses.point: Moved from Hasan to Mele for the B045 trio, stresses the stable interpretation of band topology, and ranks B022 as first alternative but doubts a metrological result is a new class of phenomena.
responses.response: Your change from Hasan to Mele is the right call on credit: the Z2 theory is a joint Kane and Mele result and I would not defend a prize that drops him. I also accept your point that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal cannot be made to disappear by wording; you say it is the reason the experiment was done in HgTe, and I agree it is a fairness cost, not a footnote. On your category worry, I would say that a class of phenomena is not the only thing the statute recognises. In 2018 and 2023 we honoured methods that opened new regimes of measurement, and lattice clocks belong there. Your question about whether the redefinition of the second is a precondition is fair; my answer is no, but I would see it as strengthening the case if it happens soon.

responses.point: As chair, ranks B022 first with Katori and Ye, and notes that Lemonde, Takamoto, Hollberg, Derevianko and the JILA team are outside the credit and that the Katori and Ye groups contest the 10^-18 regime.
responses.response: I agree with you on the configuration, and I also agree that the contest over who first reached 10^-18 is the weakest point of our own case. My answer is that the prize would be for the idea and its realisation, not for the first record, and the citation should say so. That means describing the magic-wavelength lattice rather than a number as the discovery, and I would now put the 10^-18 figure after the architecture in the wording so that no priority claim about the record is made by the Academy. I would also not make the redefinition of the second part of the citation, since that is a decision of the metrology bodies. Your own breadth objection, that B045 and B030 influence more of condensed matter, is a point I am keeping alive in my alternatives.

responses.point: Ranks B022 first, discloses a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and notes Jun Ye is a Hall-lineage JILA scientist, saying the committee may need to consider recusal.
responses.response: I appreciate that you raised this yourself. Based on what you describe, a lineage tie and no direct collaboration with Katori or Ye is a disclosed bias, not a conflict that requires you to leave the room, but it is for the committee as a whole to decide and I would support whichever course the chair and you prefer. I note that it makes it more important that the B022 case is not carried by the four B022 votes: my own position rests on the physics and on the attribution, and I would be comfortable if the B045 members tested that case hard in the final vote. As for my own Chalmers link, it concerns B039 only, and I do not read it as bearing on B022, B045 or B030.

responses.point: Treats the Lemonde, Takamoto and NIST, PTB and SYRTE contributions as the attribution test and proposes to answer it through the citation rather than by adding laureates.
responses.response: I agree with answering through the citation rather than adding names, since the three-person limit would otherwise force us to dilute the Katori and Ye credit. I also share your caution that a clock prize must not read as a verdict on all optical clocks, and your admission that atomic-physics closeness may inflate the ranking is one I take seriously for myself as well: as a microscopist I am further from the field, but I may be drawn to a clear instrument-level result because that is how I work. That is a reason to keep B045 and B030 in view as alternatives, not to relax them.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards a metrology invention as a discovery or invention in the sense of the statute when B045 offers a broader conceptual result, and how much weight breadth of influence should carry against attribution clarity.

Whether a two-name prize can be defended against Lemonde, Takamoto and the Yb and Hg groups, and whether the Katori and Ye dispute over who first reached 10^-18 can be neutralised by wording the citation around the architecture.

Whether a topological prize limited to the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 classification can stand without the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, which is the only point that could still move me toward B045.
My recollection of priority histories for B045 and B030 is from memory and has not been checked against sources here.
statement.conflict_note: I have no documented tie to Katori, Ye or any credited name on B022, B045 or B030. I share Chalmers with Goran Johansson, who directs WACQT; that link bears only on B039 and I would regard it as a disclosed bias there. Kroll's Hall-lineage tie bears on B022, and I defer to the committee on how it is handled.
